questions.q: What does production code primarily optimize for, in contrast to research code?
options: Robustness — keeping working correctly under unattended operation and unexpected inputs
Minimizing total lines of code
Using the newest available libraries
Avoiding any use of configuration files
questions.explain: Production code runs unattended and serves real users or decisions, so it is optimized for robustness: error handling, validation, and graceful degradation. Research code instead optimizes for iteration speed.

questions.q: Why is duplicating a training loop across two experiment variants sometimes the better choice than building a shared abstraction?
options: Duplication is always better than abstraction in any codebase
A premature shared abstraction is often wrong about what the second use case actually needs, and building it costs iteration speed
Git cannot track duplicated files correctly
Python does not support code reuse
questions.explain: A general abstraction built from a single use case is frequently a wrong guess about future requirements. Copy-pasting and adjusting is often faster and safer until a real pattern across multiple uses emerges.

questions.q: Which scenario is an example of premature engineering actively hurting a research team?
options: Adding a quick sanity check before running an overnight sweep
Writing a README with reproduction commands
Insisting on 90%+ unit test coverage for a training script that gets substantially rewritten every week
Logging the config used for each run
questions.explain: Comprehensive test coverage on code that changes completely every week becomes a maintenance tax rather than a safety net, since the tests are constantly invalidated by the next rewrite — slowing iteration without protecting against real risk.

questions.q: Which signal indicates that a piece of research code has crossed the line into 'worth refactoring now'?
options: It was written more than one week ago
It uses a for loop instead of a list comprehension
Multiple researchers now build experiments on top of it, so a bug in it would corrupt everyone's results
It has fewer than 50 lines
questions.explain: Once code becomes load-bearing for multiple people — or feeds a headline result — the cost of a bug or a messy shortcut now extends beyond its original author, which is the signal that real engineering investment has become worthwhile.

questions.q: Which kind of technical debt is described as genuinely acceptable to carry in research code?
options: Skipping input validation on an internal-only function where you are the only caller and control every call site
Never logging which config produced a given result
Shipping a model to real users with no monitoring
Letting a production payment service silently swallow errors
questions.explain: When you are the only caller of a function and control every call site, exhaustive input validation is pure overhead with no real benefit — a reasonable shortcut to take while iterating.
